changedBeliefs: We believed, on exp 249's evidence, that batching stream reruns was rejected because batching stream reruns hurts latency. Claim 287.2 splits that: exp 249's regression was the indivisible reply specifically, not batching. Holding its batching policy byte-identical and making only the reply divisible reverses the heterogeneous p50 it was rejected on from +66% to -9%..-52% in 4/4 passes. A rejection's stated mechanism is not often testable; this one was, and it held.

We believed per-rerun isolate messaging was a plausible share of fan-out cost -- exp 136 measured the main-isolate reader port handler at 28.57% of A11c-overlap wall and ~18 us per completion, and exp 283 left 13 of every 21 us of rerun wall unattributed. Claim 287.1 removes messaging as an explanation for the drain: cutting request messages 24:1 and replies 4:1 moves backlog drain +2.0% pooled with the sign flipping across the order flip, inside a +/-5% control floor. Exp 136's per-completion figure remains a real main-isolate cost; what changes is that it does not gate the fan-out's wall.

We believed exp 283's open question -- 'whether the reader pool is the fan-out constraint at all' -- needed a pool-size sweep to answer. It still does for the pool half, but the messaging half is now closed by claim 287.1, and the zero-ceiling control adds the other bound worth carrying: the write burst alone is 1.75 ms of the 6.03 ms drain, so a fan-out candidate that leaves both the writes and the readers' SQLite work untouched has about 4 ms to play for and, on this evidence, no share of it in dispatch.

New, and load-bearing for any future worker protocol rather than for this direction: claim 287.4 records that splitting one logical completion across several isolate turns re-opens invariants the scalar path holds by construction, because its whole completion runs in one synchronous turn inside the port handler. Two distinct hazards, one of which leaves a stream permanently stale rather than merely slow. Neither is specific to batching; both apply to any streaming, chunked, or partial-reply reader protocol.

claims.text: Per-rerun isolate messaging is not what fan-out backlog drain is made of. A candidate that packs a dirtied stream set into one message per reader worker and replies once per *changed* member turned 10,400 rerun request sends into 432 (24:1) and eliminated 7,905 of 10,400 replies (76% of members were unchanged and sent nothing), and moved the drain from 6.033 ms to 6.155 ms pooled -- +2.0%, with per-pass deltas of +11.1%, -3.0%, +3.7%, -2.5% flipping sign with arm order. The zero-ceiling control, the identical write burst with nothing subscribed, reads -5.2% and +0.7%, so every fan-out delta is inside the collection's own floor. The bound is tight because the intervention was large: there is no plausible reading in which removing 96% of a cost leaves it undetectable and the cost is material.
claims.conditions: arm64 macOS 26.2 (Darwin 25.2.0, Apple silicon), Dart 3.12.2, AOT via `dart build cli`, baseline and candidate built from separate worktrees and run as separate processes with the arm order flipped between passes (exp 249: never A/B stream dispatch with an in-process toggle). Fan-out lane: 100 streams over 100-row partitions of one table, 200 concurrent writes per burst, 5 warmup + 21 sampled bursts per pass, timed by exp 283's sentinel stream on a partition the burst never touches. Host load average 1.7-2.1

claims.text: Exp 249 was rejected by its reply protocol, not by its batching. Holding exp 249's flush policy byte-identical -- individual dispatch below pool size, one group per free worker, 64-member cap, 256-row cost gate -- and changing only the reply, so each changed member is sent the instant it is decoded and unchanged members send nothing, reverses the gate that killed it: heterogeneous single-write emission p50 goes from exp 249's +66% to -52.2%, -52.0%, -13.2%, -9.3% across four order-flipped passes, and homogeneous p50 from +22% to -45.9%, -45.2% and +9.4% in the three non-warmup passes. The metric exp 249 died on now favours the candidate; it is the throughput premise underneath (claim 287.1) that fails instead.
claims.conditions: arm64 macOS 26.2 (Darwin 25.2.0, Apple silicon), Dart 3.12.2, AOT via `dart build cli`, separate worktrees and separate processes, arm order flipped between passes. `benchmark/experiments/stream_rerun_latency.dart --trials=60`, 4 passes per collection, both scenarios: homogeneous 100 x ~100-row partitions, heterogeneous 10 x ~2000-row + 90 x ~100-row. One write dirties all 100 streams and changes exactly one; timed from write issue to that stream's emission. Host load average 1.7-2.1

claims.text: Un-batchable entries must not be allowed to take the whole worker budget ahead of the batchable majority. Exp 249's flush dispatches entries above its row-count cost gate individually and *first*, decrementing the free-worker count as it goes; because the dirty set is enumerated in stream-registration order, ten large partitions registered before ninety small ones consumed every worker and left the small majority queued behind their re-hashes. Measured at +74% to +90% on heterogeneous p50, reproduced 4/4, and reversed to a 4/4 win by splitting the free workers between the two classes. The unbatched path cannot exhibit this because it pulls from a single FIFO. Anyone reusing exp 249's `_flushQueue` inherits the defect.
claims.conditions: arm64 macOS 26.2 (Darwin 25.2.0, Apple silicon), Dart 3.12.2, AOT via `dart build cli`, separate worktrees and separate processes, arm order flipped between passes. `benchmark/experiments/stream_rerun_latency.dart --trials=60`, 4 passes per collection, both scenarios: homogeneous 100 x ~100-row partitions, heterogeneous 10 x ~2000-row + 90 x ~100-row. One write dirties all 100 streams and changes exactly one; timed from write issue to that stream's emission. Host load average 1.7-2.1

claims.text: A worker protocol that splits one logical completion across several isolate turns must re-establish, explicitly, every invariant the scalar path was holding by running its completion in one synchronous turn. Two hazards found in the streaming-batch prototype, both properties of the protocol rather than of the code: (a) a member whose result is unchanged sends no reply at all, and `StreamEngine.onDependencyChanges` skips queueing anything already `inFlight`, so a member re-dirtied mid-batch is invisible to both and the stream stays stale until an unrelated later write happens to dirty it again -- reproduced as a non-converging stream by a test issuing overlapping write waves; (b) re-queueing a re-dirtied member from inside the partial handler makes it simultaneously queued and in-flight, so a concurrent write's `_flushQueue` can dispatch a second rerun over the same hash baseline while the worker still holds the first. The fix for both is to defer requeueing to the terminator, where in-flight is released in the same turn.
claims.conditions: Found by construction and by a convergence test (20 streams, three overlapping write waves, each wave dirtying every stream) against the exp 287 prototype at `archive/exp-287`; both hazards are reasoned from the protocol shape and (a) is reproduced as a test failure

claims.text: Tail emission latency under batched reruns is unresolved and this run does not decide it. p95 moved positive in 11 of 16 pass-deltas, which matches what static chunk assignment would predict -- a member at the end of a long chunk cannot be taken by a worker that has gone idle, which a FIFO always permits -- but the two collections disagree on the homogeneous scenario (+29.6/+52.2/+24.4, then +89.1/+196.2/-54.4/-50.6) and a 120-trial read of the whole distribution does not separate the arms at p90 or p95 in either scenario. One candidate sample reached 14.1 ms against a baseline maximum of 4.2 ms. Do not cite this as a measured regression; the rejection rests on claim 287.1.
claims.conditions: arm64 macOS 26.2 (Darwin 25.2.0, Apple silicon), Dart 3.12.2, AOT via `dart build cli`, separate worktrees and separate processes, arm order flipped between passes. `benchmark/experiments/stream_rerun_latency.dart --trials=60`, 4 passes per collection, both scenarios: homogeneous 100 x ~100-row partitions, heterogeneous 10 x ~2000-row + 90 x ~100-row. One write dirties all 100 streams and changes exactly one; timed from write issue to that stream's emission. Host load average 1.7-2.1; plus two 120-trial single-shot runs per arm per scenario read at p50/p75/p90/p95/p99/max

nextSignals: Do not open a fourth batching candidate in this direction. Claim 287.1 measures the entire ceiling that adaptive sizing, work stealing, cheaper terminators or per-member priorities would compete for, and it is zero on the representative fan-out lane. The one shape that would reopen it is a fan-out of very cheap streams -- one-row partitions, where exp 283's 4.54 us hash pass shrinks toward the dispatch cost instead of dwarfing it.

Exp 283's suggested probe is now the obvious next one and this run narrows it: sweep the reader pool size across one drain burst. Claim 287.1 removes messaging as the explanation for the fan-out wall and the control puts the write burst at 1.75 ms of 6.03 ms, so the sweep is asking whether the remaining ~4 ms is reader-side parallelism or something serial on the main isolate. It needs no new runtime code.

Method worth reusing, and the run's most transferable output: to test whether X is a system's constraint, building the version with almost none of X and watching the wall not move bounds X more tightly than instrumenting X does. A 24:1 message reduction that changes nothing is a stronger statement about dispatch overhead than any per-call counter, and it cost one build.

Claim 287.4 is a standing constraint on any future streaming, chunked, or partial-reply reader protocol -- not only on batching. The specific trap is the entry that is both queued and in-flight, a state the scalar path cannot reach.

`benchmark/experiments/stream_rerun_latency.dart` has now caught two distinct defects in two experiments (exp 249's verdict, and this run's flush-policy starvation in its first collection). Keep running it on any stream-dispatch change, and keep both of its scenarios: the heterogeneous one is what caught the defect.
outcomeNote: Moonshot. The mechanism worked and the prize was not there. Streaming the batch's replies reverses the emission-latency regression exp 249 was rejected for, confirming that rejection's own account of itself; with the reply fixed, cutting fan-out rerun messages 24:1 and replies 4:1 moves backlog drain by nothing, which closes the batching family from the throughput side that exp 249 never measured. Runtime reverted, prototype at `archive/exp-287`.
